units.translation: 156-60a. And with them Periclymenus: that Periclymenus was the son of Neleus is clear. For the poet says (Od. 11.286): 'Nestor and Chromius and lordly Periclymenus.' Poseidon, as his descendant—for Neleus was the son of Poseidon—both adorned him among the others and granted him the ability to change into all things, as Euphorion also says (fr. 74 Scheidw.): 'who was like to all things, a sea-creature like Proteus.'

Heracles killed him when he had changed into a fly in the war against the Pylians, striking him with his club on the advice of Athena, 〈...〉 stuck like a bee with its sting. But Hesiod (fr. 14 Rz.²) says that he changed into one of his customary forms and sat upon the navel of the yoke of Heracles' horses, wishing to engage in battle with the hero, and that Heracles shot him fatally with an arrow when Athena pointed him out. He speaks thus: 'and lordly Periclymenus, blessed, to whom Poseidon the Earth-shaker gave gifts of all kinds: at one time he would appear among birds as an eagle, at another he would become—a wonder to behold—an ant, at another the splendid tribes of bees, at another a dread and pitiless serpent. He had gifts of all kinds, not to be named, which later deceived him by the counsel of Athena.'

b. 〈Pylos:〉 from which Nestor came, which is also sandy from the river flowing past. Neleus had sons: from Chloris, Nestor, Periclymenus, Chromius; and from various women, Taurus, Asterius, Pylaon, Deimachus, Eurybius, Epileon, Phrasis, Antimenes, Euagoras, or, as Asclepiades (12 fr. 21 J.) says, Alastor. And the poet (Il. 11.692): 'for we were twelve sons of blameless Neleus.'

161-63. They who Tegea: Tegea is a city of Arcadia. And 〈the portion of Apheidas〉 means the kingdom of Apheidas. For Aleus is said to be the son of Apheidas, son of Arcas, from whom the land is called Arcadia. Apheidas, son of Arcas, an ancient hero, ruled over Tegea. There are two Cepheuses: one the son of Aleus, whom Apollonius mentions, and the other 〈...〉, whom Hellanicus mentions in his work On Arcadia (4 fr. 37 J.).
